screens.title: Getting Started with C# and Your First Script
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we'll connect what a game object is to what a C# script does. C# is the primary language Unity uses to express behavior: movement, rules, user input and the logic that makes your game respond. You will learn how to create a C# script asset, open it in your editor, attach it as a component to a GameObject, and run a tiny program that prints to the Unity Console. This step shows you the full loop: author code, attach it, run the scene, and inspect output. That loop is the fastest way to learn. I'll also preview variables and the two most common lifecycle methods you will use at the start: Start and Update. By the end of this chapter you will have a working script that prints messages and holds simple data like health and speed. As you follow the hands-on steps, notice how public fields appear in the Inspector so designers can tweak values without changing code. Think of this session as opening the door to iterating quickly: small code, immediate feedback, and faster playtesting. Are you ready to create your first script and see C# drive a GameObject?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical, hands-on skills you will use while developing in Unity. First, you will understand the role of C# as the scripting language that defines behavior for GameObjects. That means you can explain why movement, UI updates, and simple AI come from scripts. Second, you will create a C# script asset, name it with PascalCase, open it in your editor, and attach it to a GameObject so it runs in play mode. Third, you will read and write the basic C# structure Unity provides: using directives, a public class inheriting from MonoBehaviour, and the common lifecycle methods. Finally on this screen you will begin using Debug. Log to inspect runtime values, a quick debugging habit that saves time. Each objective is hands-on and testable: create a script, attach it, and verify Console output. As you practice, focus on the why: public fields expose tuning in the Inspector; Start is for setup; Update for repeated checks. These are core patterns you'll use in almost every Unity script.

screens.title: What C# Does in a Unity Project
screens.narratorSegment: C# is the programming language you use to tell Unity what to do. In Unity, a script is simply a C# class that usually inherits from MonoBehaviour so it can be attached as a component to a GameObject. That connection is essential: the GameObject provides the identity and transform in the scene; the C# script supplies methods and data that change that object's behavior over time. A clear example is player movement: the GameObject represents the player model, while a PlayerController script reads input and modifies the Transform to move the model each frame. This separation — data and identity in the GameObject, behavior in scripts — helps you keep responsibilities clear when projects grow. A common misconception is that GameObjects themselves do logic; they do not. The logic lives in scripts. Another useful distinction: C# is object-oriented, so scripts are classes that can hold fields (variables) and methods; fields can be public to expose tuning in the Inspector. Why this matters: by centralizing behavior in C# you can version control your logic, write unit tests when needed, and let non-programmers tweak values via the Inspector. Reflect: what behavior would you separate into a script versus a built-in component?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A C# script is the behavioral component for a GameObject; it organizes logic and data while Unity manages objects and rendering.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What C# Does
C# as the behavioral layer
Scripts hold logic and data; GameObjects hold identity and transform.
Key points
  • Scripts are C# classes that usually inherit from MonoBehaviour to attach to GameObjects.
  • Fields in scripts store data; methods implement behavior executed by Unity at runtime.
  • Public fields show in the Inspector so designers can tweak values without code changes.
Analogy
Think of a GameObject as a car body in a garage and scripts as the engine and wiring that make it drive and signal.
Key Takeaway

Scripts separate behavior from objects: code controls how GameObjects act at runtime.

Concrete example: Player movement
A PlayerController script reads input and updates Transform.position. The player model is a GameObject; the script is the behavior attached to it.
Common misconception
Some beginners expect GameObjects to store logic. In Unity, most custom logic belongs in scripts; built-in components provide physics and rendering.
Reflect
Which behavior in your game should be a script and which can be handled by built-in components?

screens.title: Create, Name, and Attach a C# Script
screens.narratorSegment: Creating and attaching a C# script in Unity is a precise but simple process. First, in the Project window open the Assets folder. Right-click, choose Create, then C# Script to make a new script asset. Name it with PascalCase — for example PlayerController — because Unity will use the filename to find the class. If the class name and file name don't match, Unity will warn you or fail to compile. Second, double-click the script to open it in your configured editor such as Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code. Editors provide syntax highlighting and IntelliSense which speeds learning and prevents typos. Third, drag the script asset from the Project window onto a GameObject in the Hierarchy or Inspector to attach it as a component. Once attached, the script becomes part of that GameObject and will participate in lifecycle callbacks. A common mistake is creating the asset but not attaching it; nothing runs until a script is attached. Another trap is renaming the file but not the class, which creates a mismatch. Practice these steps until they become second nature because attaching scripts is how you connect code to the scene.

Step-by-step

  2. Right-click → Create → C# Script and name it with PascalCase (e.g., PlayerController).
  3. Double-click the script to open your editor and observe the boilerplate code.

screens.title: Understanding the Default Script Boilerplate
screens.narratorSegment: When you open a freshly created C# script in Unity you'll see a small boilerplate that sets the stage for everything you write. At the top, using directives such as using UnityEngine import namespaces containing Unity-specific classes and types. Below that you will find a public class whose name matches the file; it usually inherits from MonoBehaviour which exposes Unity lifecycle callbacks and lets the script be added as a component. Inside the class there are methods like Start and Update. Start runs once before the first frame and is ideal for initializing variables or finding references to other GameObjects. Update runs every frame and is used for continuous checks like input or movement. A common misconception is to overload Start with per-frame logic — that belongs in Update. Another issue is removing using UnityEngine; without it types like GameObject and Transform will not be found by the compiler. Understanding each boilerplate piece helps you extend scripts safely and locate errors quickly. Understanding the Default Script Boilerplate means the default script wires namespaces, a monobehaviour class, and lifecycle methods that run at known times.. In practical terms, using directives, class declaration, monobehaviour inheritance, start and update. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Boilerplate
keyIdea.text: The default script wires namespaces, a MonoBehaviour class, and lifecycle methods that run at known times.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Boilerplate
Script anatomy
  • using UnityEngine; imports Unity types like GameObject and Debug.
  • public class Name : MonoBehaviour declares a class that can attach as a component.
  • Start() runs once before the first frame for initialization.
  • Update() runs every frame for continuous behavior.
Code example
using UnityEngine; // Imports the Unity Engine namespace

public class MyFirstScript : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Start is called before the first frame update
    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Hello, Cohortia Game Devs!");
    }

    // Update is called once per frame
    void Update()
    {
        // Per-frame logic goes here
    }
}
Note: keep the file name and public class name identical so Unity compiles the script.

screens.title: Start() vs Update()
screens.narratorSegment: Start and Update are two of Unity's most used lifecycle methods and understanding their differences is vital. Start runs a single time just before the first frame where the script is enabled. Use Start for setup tasks: assign initial values, find references to other GameObjects, or initialize components. Update runs once per frame and is intended for continuous checks like reading player input, applying movement, or checking conditions that change over time. It's a common beginner mistake to put initialization code inside Update; that causes work to be repeated unnecessarily and can degrade performance. Another misconception is to place physics movement in Update — physics updates are better handled in FixedUpdate, but in this chapter we focus on Start and Update. A concrete example: set an initial health value in Start, but reduce health when damage is received inside a method called by collision or input, possibly invoked in Update. Always consider whether code needs to run once or repeatedly before choosing the method. Start() vs Update() means start runs once for initialization; update runs every frame for continuous logic. choose appropriately to avoid wasted work.. In practical terms, when to initialize and when to run per-frame logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Start vs Update
Start()
Runs once. Ideal for initial setup like setting health, finding references, or initializing UI.
  • Called before the first frame when the script is enabled.
  • Good for non-repeating tasks and initial state.
Update()
Runs every frame. Use for input handling, movement, and polling values that change frequently.
  • Called each frame; keep code efficient to avoid performance issues.
  • Avoid heavy calculations; consider events or coroutines when appropriate.
Example scenario
Set player health = 100 in Start. In Update, check for input to move the player and only reduce health when damage occurs. Initialization should not be repeated in Update.
Key Takeaway

Decide if code runs once or every frame; place accordingly in Start or Update to keep logic correct and performant.

screens.title: Using Debug.Log() to Inspect Runtime Values
screens.narratorSegment: Debug. Log is one of the simplest and most powerful tools when you're starting. By printing messages and variable values to the Unity Console you can verify that code executed, inspect variable state, and trace the flow of execution without stepping through a debugger. Use Debug. Log("Message") for simple traces or Debug. Log("Value: " + variable) to concatenate data. For example, printing the player's position in Start confirms a correct initial location; printing health after assignment confirms the initialization worked. Remember to remove or reduce frequent logging in Update because logging every frame can flood the Console and slow the Editor. A common misconception is expecting Debug. Log to change game state — it only reports values. Also use Debug. LogWarning and Debug. LogError when you want messages that stand out or show severity. Practically, insert a few well-placed logs, run the scene, and use timestamps and message context to interpret when each log appears. This habit is the fastest route from confusion to clarity when learning scripting. Using Debug.Log() to Inspect Runtime Values means use debug.log to observe runtime behavior; avoid logging every frame and prefer contextual messages for clarity.. In practical terms, print messages and variable values to unity's console for quick feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Debug.Log()
Why use Debug.Log
  • Confirm code execution and variable values quickly.
  • Trace order of events during Play mode without a debugger.
  • Use warning and error logs to prioritize issues.
Code snippets
Debug.Log("Welcome, " + playerName);
Debug.Log("Current Score: " + playerScore);
Debug.LogWarning("Low health: " + health);
Debug.LogError("Missing component: " + componentName);
Keep logs descriptive and remove noisy logs from Update when not needed.
Practical example
In Start, print the initial values of health, speed, and name to confirm they are set as expected. In Update, avoid printing every frame; instead log only on state changes.

screens.title: Variables and Common Data Types
screens.narratorSegment: Variables are named memory locations that store values your code uses. In C#, each variable has a type that dictates what kind of data it can hold. The most common types you'll use in Unity are int for whole numbers, float for decimal numbers, string for text, and bool for true/false states. Use int for values like score or lives, float for positions, speeds, and physics-related numbers — remember float literals require an f suffix like 5.0f — string for names and messages, and bool for flags such as isAlive. Declaring a variable looks like: int score = 0; public float movementSpeed = 7.5f; string playerName = "Hero"; bool isPlayerAlive = true;. Fields declared inside the class but outside methods are accessible to all methods in the class and, if public, appear in the Inspector. Beginners often mix up types, for instance assigning a string to an int or forgetting the f suffix for floats — the compiler will report these as errors. Always initialize fields you depend on, or check for nulls and defaults to prevent unexpected behavior during runtime.

keyIdea.title: Data types
keyIdea.text: Choose types deliberately: int for integers, float for decimals, string for text, bool for true/false. Initialize fields to avoid surprises.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Variables & Types
Common types
int
Whole numbers: score, lives. Example: int score = 0;
float
Decimal numbers: speed, positions. Example: float speed = 5.0f;
string
Text: names, UI. Example: string playerName = "Hero";
bool
True/false flags. Example: bool isAlive = true;
Best practices
  • Initialize fields, especially if they won't be set in the Inspector.
  • Use descriptive names like playerHealth or movementSpeed for clarity.
  • Respect case-sensitivity: playerScore and PlayerScore are different.
Key Takeaway

Match types to data and initialize fields to avoid nulls and default surprises during runtime.

screens.title: Public Fields, the Inspector, and Why They Matter
screens.narratorSegment: Public fields let Unity expose data to the Inspector, and that is a powerful design pattern for fast iteration. When you declare a field as public in a script — for example public int health = 100; — Unity displays that field in the Inspector whenever an instance of the script is attached to a GameObject. Designers and level builders can then change values directly in the Editor without editing code or recompiling. This speeds balancing and experimentation. Keep in mind public does not only affect visibility; it also changes accessibility from other scripts. If you want Inspector visibility without public access, use [SerializeField] on a private field, but that is beyond this chapter's first steps. Beginner misconceptions include assuming public equals constant; public fields are still mutable at runtime. Also remember that Inspector values override initial values set in code for that instance once the script has been serialized on the GameObject. That behavior is useful but something to watch when initializing defaults in Start. Use public fields intentionally to separate tuning data from logic. Public Fields, the Inspector, and Why They Matter means public fields expose values in the inspector so non-programmers can tweak gameplay without changing code; use serialization wisely.. Complete code
using UnityEngine;

public class MyFirstScript : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Fields declared at class scope
    public int playerScore = 0;
    public float playerMovementSpeed = 7.5f;
    public string playerName = "Adventurer";
    public bool isPlayerAlive = true;

    void Start()
    {
        Debug.Log("Welcome, " + playerName + "!");
        Debug.Log("Current Score: " + playerScore);
        Debug.Log("Movement Speed: " + playerMovementSpeed);
        Debug.Log("Player is Alive: " + isPlayerAlive);

        // Change values at runtime
        playerScore = 100;
        playerMovementSpeed = 10.0f;
        isPlayerAlive = false;

        Debug.Log("--- After updating values ---");
        Debug.Log("New Score: " + playerScore);
        Debug.Log("New Movement Speed: " + playerMovementSpeed);
        Debug.Log("Player is Alive now: " + isPlayerAlive);
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // Empty for now
    }
}
Walkthrough notes
  • Fields are declared outside methods so Start and Update can access them.
  • Debug.Log shows initial values, then we change them and log again to verify updates.
  • This pattern helps you validate both setup and runtime state changes quickly.

Run this script and watch the Console to learn how declarations, assignments, and logs map to runtime output.

screens.narratorSegment: Beginners commonly see compile errors that block their game from running. These often come from simple syntax mistakes: missing semicolons at the end of statements, mismatched braces, or incorrect spelling and case for identifiers. C# is case-sensitive, so playerScore and playerscore are different names. Type mismatches are another frequent issue: trying to assign the text "100" to an int or forgetting the f suffix for float literals leads to compile-time errors. The Unity Console and your code editor will show error messages and the line number; read these messages carefully because they point to the problem and often suggest fixes. When you see an error, open the script in your editor, go to the line, and check the token the compiler flagged. Fixing small typos usually resolves the issue. A useful habit is incremental changes: make one small change, save, and watch the Console again. That way you isolate the change that caused a problem and learn to interpret error messages confidently. Welcome. In this lesson we'll connect what a game object is to what a C# script does. C# is the primary language Unity uses to express behavior: movement, rules, user input and the logic that makes your game respond. You will learn how to create a C# script asset, open it in your editor, attach it as a component to a GameObject, and run a tiny program that prints to the Unity Console. This step shows you the full loop: author code, attach it, run the scene, and inspect output. That loop is the fastest way to learn. I'll also preview variables and the two most common lifecycle methods you will use at the start: Start and Update. By the end of this chapter you will have a working script that prints messages and holds simple data like health and speed. As you follow the hands-on steps, notice how public fields appear in the Inspector so designers can tweak values without changing code. Think of this session as opening the door to iterating quickly: small code, immediate feedback, and faster playtesting. Are you ready to create your first script and see C# drive a GameObject?

These objectives map to practical, hands-on skills you will use while developing in Unity. First, you will understand the role of C# as the scripting language that defines behavior for GameObjects. That means you can explain why movement, UI updates, and simple AI come from scripts. Second, you will create a C# script asset, name it with PascalCase, open it in your editor, and attach it to a GameObject so it runs in play mode. Third, you will read and write the basic C# structure Unity provides: using directives, a public class inheriting from MonoBehaviour, and the common lifecycle methods. Finally on this screen you will begin using Debug. Log to inspect runtime values, a quick debugging habit that saves time. Each objective is hands-on and testable: create a script, attach it, and verify Console output. As you practice, focus on the why: public fields expose tuning in the Inspector; Start is for setup; Update for repeated checks. These are core patterns you'll use in almost every Unity script.

This second objectives page focuses on variables, inspector use, and common error correction. First, you will declare, initialize, and assign values to variables using common C# types: int, float, string, and bool. Second, you will make fields public so they appear in the Inspector, enabling non-programmer team members to tune values. Third, you will practice identifying common syntax errors such as missing semicolons, wrong data types, and case-sensitivity mistakes. Fourth on this screen you will complete a short hands-on activity that creates a CharacterStats script, attaches it to a Player GameObject, and prints initial values to the Console. C# is the programming language you use to tell Unity what to do. In Unity, a script is simply a C# class that usually inherits from MonoBehaviour so it can be attached as a component to a GameObject. That connection is essential: the GameObject provides the identity and transform in the scene; the C# script supplies methods and data that change that object's behavior over time. A clear example is player movement: the GameObject represents the player model, while a PlayerController script reads input and modifies the Transform to move the model each frame. This separation — data and identity in the GameObject, behavior in scripts — helps you keep responsibilities clear when projects grow. Why this matters: by centralizing behavior in C# you can version control your logic, write unit tests when needed, and let non-programmers tweak values via the Inspector. Creating and attaching a C# script in Unity is a precise but simple process. First, in the Project window open the Assets folder. Right-click, choose Create, then C# Script to make a new script asset. Name it with PascalCase — for example PlayerController — because Unity will use the filename to find the class. If the class name and file name don't match, Unity will warn you or fail to compile. Second, double-click the script to open it in your configured editor such as Visual Studio or Visual Studio Code. Editors provide syntax highlighting and IntelliSense which speeds learning and prevents typos. Third, drag the script asset from the Project window onto a GameObject in the Hierarchy or Inspector to attach it as a component. Once attached, the script becomes part of that GameObject and will participate in lifecycle callbacks. A common mistake is creating the asset but not attaching it; nothing runs until a script is attached. Another trap is renaming the file but not the class, which creates a mismatch. Practice these steps until they become second nature because attaching scripts is how you connect code to the scene.

At the top, using directives such as using UnityEngine import namespaces containing Unity-specific classes and types. Below that you will find a public class whose name matches the file; it usually inherits from MonoBehaviour which exposes Unity lifecycle callbacks and lets the script be added as a component. Inside the class there are methods like Start and Update. Start runs once before the first frame and is ideal for initializing variables or finding references to other GameObjects. Update runs every frame and is used for continuous checks like input or movement. A common misconception is to overload Start with per-frame logic — that belongs in Update. Another issue is removing using UnityEngine; without it types like GameObject and Transform will not be found by the compiler. Understanding each boilerplate piece helps you extend scripts safely and locate errors quickly. These often come from simple syntax mistakes: missing semicolons at the end of statements, mismatched braces, or incorrect spelling and case for identifiers. C# is case-sensitive, so playerScore and playerscore are different names. Type mismatches are another frequent issue: trying to assign the text "100" to an int or forgetting the f suffix for float literals leads to compile-time errors. The Unity Console and your code editor will show error messages and the line number; read these messages carefully because they point to the problem and often suggest fixes. When you see an error, open the script in your editor, go to the line, and check the token the compiler flagged. Fixing small typos usually resolves the issue.
